bp: Online debate is now one of the places where societies argue over elections, health, climate, war, identity, and policy. The object being studied is not just a sentence on a page. It is a public exchange made of claims, reasons, replies, agreement, disagreement, bias, and attempts to persuade. BeyondFacts'26 serves the need to read that exchange at a scale no newsroom, fact-checking group, or social science team can handle by hand. The workshop's premise is that machines can help find claims, detect which side a speaker takes, and check factual support, but only if the task is defined carefully. A claim has meaning inside a debate; an argument depends on what evidence it offers; an opinion may be honest disagreement or part of a misleading pattern. The workshop therefore treats online discourse analysis as a meeting point between web mining, artificial intelligence, language processing, journalism, communication studies, political science, and computer science.
wh: The hard part is that public discourse is not a clean pile of true and false statements. People quote others, imply things without saying them directly, use sarcasm, mix facts with values, and shift meaning as a conversation unfolds. Misinformation, disinformation, bias, and echo chambers make the problem worse because the same sentence can play different roles in different communities. A fact-checking tool may ask whether a statement matches evidence, while a stance detector asks whether a speaker supports or rejects it, and an argument miner asks what reason is being offered. Those are related tasks, but they are not interchangeable. If the system treats them as one flat classification problem, it can miss the difference between an unsupported factual claim, a value judgment, and a strategic reply. The abstract also stresses conceptual foundations, which means the main difficulty is not only technical accuracy. It is defining what counts as a claim, an argument, an opinion, or a verified fact in socially contested settings.
naive: A smart beginner would collect social media posts about a contentious issue, search for suspicious words, and send every flagged sentence to a fact checker or text classifier. That is a reasonable first move because misinformation and bias often do leave visible language clues. It fails because online debate is relational. A post may be false only because it removes context. A reply may look hostile but actually be challenging a harmful claim. A repeated phrase may indicate an echo chamber, or it may be a shared slogan in a legitimate movement. Keyword rules also cannot separate a claim from the evidence offered for it, or a stance from the topic itself. The result is a noisy alert stream that scales poorly and gives little explanation of why a debate is being distorted.
ap: The core idea is to make online discourse analysis an explicitly interdisciplinary machine-reading problem. Instead of treating text analysis as a tool that can be dropped onto public debate unchanged, the workshop asks researchers to combine computational methods with theories of communication and social life. In concrete terms, that means separating several moving parts: what claim is being made, what argument supports it, what stance the speaker takes, what evidence can verify it, and what social pattern may amplify it. Language-processing methods provide scale, because they can scan many posts, comments, articles, and replies. Social science and journalism provide the categories that keep the machine from confusing surface language with social meaning. The central move is therefore not a single model. It is a research program for building systems whose units of analysis match the real structure of debate: claims, arguments, opinions, evidence, bias, misinformation, disinformation, and echo chambers.
mech: The mechanism begins with online discourse: posts, comments, articles, replies, or other web text around contentious issues. First, the text must be divided into interpretable units. One unit may be a factual claim, another may be a reason supporting that claim, another may be a statement of agreement or rejection. Second, each unit is given a role. Argument mining looks for pieces of reasoning: what is asserted, what evidence is offered, and how the pieces connect. Stance detection asks which side a speaker appears to take toward a target claim or issue. Fact verification asks whether outside evidence supports, contradicts, or leaves the claim unresolved. Third, these outputs have to be placed back into a social setting. If many users repeat the same unsupported claim inside a tight community, the system may reveal an echo chamber. If one side's arguments are consistently represented differently from another's, the system may reveal bias. Fourth, researchers compare these machine outputs with conceptual standards from communication studies, political science, computational journalism, and computer science. The final output is not merely a label on a sentence. It is a more structured reading of a debate: which claims circulate, who supports or resists them, what reasons are used, what evidence bears on them, and where harmful information patterns may be forming.
math: The mathematical ideas are measurement, classification, comparison, and networked evidence, but each has to be understood plainly. Measurement means deciding what observable signs count as evidence for a hidden social role: a claim, an argument, a stance, or a verification status. Classification means drawing boundaries among roles, while accepting that real language often sits near a boundary. Comparison means judging whether a new sentence resembles earlier examples whose roles were known, and choosing which differences matter. For stance, the important comparison is between the words in the post and the target issue: does the speaker move toward support, rejection, or uncertainty? For fact verification, probability is the everyday idea of changing confidence when evidence is partial or conflicting. A source may support one part of a claim and not another, so the system should not become more certain than the evidence allows. Graph reasoning can also appear because debates have participants, replies, citations, and communities as connected objects; evidence may travel through links, but misleading links can spread bad signals. The tradeoff is scale versus interpretation. Mathematical scoring lets researchers inspect large debate spaces, but the scores must be tied to carefully defined concepts or they become precise-looking numbers attached to vague social categories.
dots: This workshop sits directly between the repo's text mining and misinformation-trust families. Like fact-checking papers, it treats public claims as objects that need evidence before they can be trusted. Like misinformation correction and detection work, it recognizes that falsehood is not only a sentence-level property; it is shaped by persuasion, intent, audience, and repetition. It also connects to social network and influence work because echo chambers are not created by isolated posts. They arise when people, platforms, and communities repeatedly pass selected evidence to one another. The recurring conference ideas are ranking, probability, graphs, and language models, but here they serve a broader interpretive task. Ranking helps prioritize which claims deserve attention. Probability helps keep uncertainty visible. Graphs describe how replies and communities carry influence. Language models can parse and generate language, but the workshop's emphasis on conceptual foundations warns that fluent text processing is not enough. The paper is therefore a connective venue for methods that often appear separately.
ww: The approach should work because it matches the layered nature of discourse. The naive approach asks one question at a time, such as whether a sentence is false, and loses the surrounding structure. BeyondFacts'26 starts from the fact that public debate has several layers at once: factual content, argumentative form, speaker position, evidence, community circulation, and social meaning. When those layers are separated, each task becomes less confused. A system can ask whether a sentence makes a checkable claim before it asks whether the claim is true. It can ask whether a reply agrees or disagrees before interpreting the reply as part of an echo chamber. It can ask whether an argument offers evidence or only repeats a slogan. Interdisciplinary grounding improves this process because social scientists, political scientists, journalists, and computer scientists notice different failure modes. A purely computational view may scale but misdefine the target. A purely manual view may understand the target but cannot follow millions of exchanges. Combining them keeps both reach and meaning in view.
po: The payoff is a stronger research base for machine-based interpretation of societal debates. Grounded in the abstract, the workshop brings together communities that normally study different pieces of the same problem: language processing, web mining, artificial intelligence, communication, political life, journalism, and computer science. It focuses attention on practical capabilities such as finding arguments, detecting stance, verifying facts, and studying misinformation, disinformation, bias, and echo chambers. The gain is not a single deployed detector. It is a shared place to define the tasks well enough that later tools can help journalists, researchers, platforms, and civic institutions understand contested online issues at scale.
limits: Because this is a workshop description, the abstract does not prove a particular method, dataset, accuracy level, or deployment result. It names important tasks and communities, but it does not specify how claims are labeled, how disagreement is handled, how evidence is retrieved, or how bias and echo chambers are measured. The approach assumes that interdisciplinary categories can be made precise enough for machine analysis without losing the social meaning that made them useful. It also assumes that available online data is representative enough to study societal debates, even though platforms, languages, moderation rules, and participation patterns can distort what is visible. The strongest reading is therefore agenda-setting rather than empirical proof.
